title: C1102 — Horn connector reference
introduction:
The housing outline is this horn connector's silhouette; the identity table is its name tag. I use them together before reading the electrical details, because a familiar-looking plug is only the start of identification. Follow the printed cavity labels from the drawing into the pin table, then read across the matching row.

The identity table's Color belongs to the housing, while Color in the pin assignments belongs to the wire. Each cavity row brings together a circuit identifier, wire information, function and terminal reference. The pigtail table then connects the connector's shell reference with its listed service part.

This is a connector-reading reference. Physical viewing direction, access, probing, electrical test conditions and replacement methods require separate workshop information. Size and Used remain unexplained codes, and the Gauge entries remain in their original convention without conversion.

edits.why: The drawing has a rectangular upper feature and an asymmetric outer shoulder. I use those visible details to keep track of the illustrated layout, then let the cavity labels identify the contacts. The Fpn and Harness Id beneath the picture associate it with the recorded connector. The illustration does not specify a physical viewing side.

Read across a cavity's row to distinguish circuit identity from circuit function and to keep its wire and terminal details together. The ground description identifies the listed return path; the horn-relay description identifies the other electrical role. A relay is an electrically controlled switch, and its appearance in a function label does not prove that it is a separate plug-in component.

A pigtail combines a connector with attached wire leads. Kit List connects the identity table to Number here, and Engineering Shell can be compared with Hard Shell. I distinguish those shell references from Service Part and the Image filename. The pigtail's Gauge field is a separate entry from the circuit-row gauges, not permission to substitute wire or begin a splice.
